choices: a full moon and a clear sky
the moon to be at its farthest point
a new moon lined up exactly between the sun and Earth
Earth to pass between the sun and the moon
review.why: The moon must sit directly between Earth and the sun, which happens only at some new moons.

review.q: Which object has almost all of the mass in the solar system?
review.why: The sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass, which is why everything orbits it.

review.q: Looking at a galaxy 50 million light-years away shows it
choices: as it was 50 million years ago
as it will be in 50 million years
review.why: Light takes 50 million years to arrive, so we see the galaxy's past.

review.q: In undisturbed layers, a fossil in a lower layer is
choices: the same age as one above it
review.why: Superposition: lower layers formed first, so their fossils are older.

review.q: Which rock gives the most direct radiometric age?
review.why: Igneous rock sets its atomic clock when it cools; sedimentary rock is dated by bracketing.

review.q: About how old is Earth, according to radiometric dating of the oldest rocks and meteorites?
review.why: Meteorites and the oldest rocks give ages near 4.5 billion years by several independent methods.

chapters.title: Earth and Human Activity
chapters.bigQuestion: How do people depend on Earth's resources, how are we changing the planet, and what does the evidence say we should do?

story.title: The Water That a City Drinks
story.kicker: Every glass of water in Chicago starts two miles out in Lake Michigan, and keeping it clean once meant turning a river around.
paragraphs: Stand on the Chicago lakefront and look east. A few kilometers out, you can see small round buildings sitting on the water. They are water intake cribs. Below each one, a tunnel runs under the lake floor back to shore. Lake water flows in, gets filtered and treated at two enormous purification plants, and then flows through thousands of kilometers of pipes to homes across the city and dozens of suburbs. Millions of people drink Lake Michigan every day.

It was not always safe to do so. In the 1800s Chicago dumped its sewage into the Chicago River, and the river flowed into the lake, right where the city took its drinking water. Waves of typhoid and cholera killed thousands. Engineers pushed the intake cribs farther and farther offshore, but the lake kept getting dirtier.

So the city did something no one had tried at that scale. Between 1892 and 1900 it dug a canal 45 kilometers long and deep enough to reverse the river. When the last dam was opened in January 1900, the Chicago River began to flow backward, away from the lake and toward the Mississippi. The sewage went with it, downstream toward St. Louis, whose residents were not pleased. Chicago's water got cleaner. The problem had moved, not vanished.

Today the lake is far cleaner than it was a century ago, thanks to treatment plants, laws and constant testing. But it is not unlimited. The Great Lakes hold about one fifth of the fresh surface water on Earth, yet only about one percent of that is renewed each year by rain and snow. The rest is a gift from melting glaciers that ended more than ten thousand years ago. Draw it down faster than it refills and it does not come back.

Lake Michigan is a small version of a planet-sized question. People need water, minerals, energy and land. Earth has them, but not everywhere and not without end. Taking them changes the air, the water and the ground. This chapter looks at what the evidence says about those changes and about how people are learning to take less and waste less.
story.think: Reversing the river sent Chicago's sewage toward other people downstream. Was that a solution or just a relocation? What would a real solution look like?

lessons.title: Where Minerals Come From
lessons.mainIdea: Useful minerals collect only where certain geologic processes happened, so they are found in some places and not others.
reading: Your phone holds copper, gold, lithium, cobalt and a dozen other metals. None of them are spread evenly through Earth's crust. Most rock holds only a tiny trace. A *mineral resource* is a place where a natural process concentrated a useful mineral enough to be worth digging up. That concentrated rock is called *ore*.

The processes are slow and specific. Hot water moving through cracks in cooling magma dissolves metals and drops them in veins, which is where most gold and copper come from. Rivers sort heavy grains and pile them in gravel beds. Ancient shallow seas evaporated and left beds of salt. Illinois has no gold, but it has some of the largest deposits of fluorite in the country in the far south, where hot fluids once seeped up along faults. Fluorite is the Illinois state mineral.

Because ore forms only in certain places, countries and regions end up with very different resources. Chile has copper. Australia has iron. A few countries hold most of the world's cobalt. That unevenness drives trade, and sometimes conflict. It also means that once a deposit is mined out, there is no growing it back. Minerals are *nonrenewable* on any human time scale.

The other side of the story is reuse. Copper in an old wire is as good as copper from a mine. Recycling metals uses far less energy than smelting new ore and creates far less waste rock. Geologists now talk about the urban mine: the metal already sitting in cities, waiting to be collected.

words.d: a natural concentration of a useful mineral that people can mine
rock that holds enough of a valuable mineral to be worth mining
a resource that is not replaced by nature within a human lifetime

look.title: Two Hillsides
look.text: Two hills look the same from the road. Both are made of granite. Under one, millions of years ago, hot water rich in dissolved copper moved up through cracks and cooled. Under the other, nothing like that happened. Today a mining company tests both.
look.prompt: Which hill is worth mining and why? What does this tell you about why resources are unevenly spread?

check.q: What makes rock count as ore?
choices: It holds enough of a valuable mineral to be worth mining
It is found near a city
check.why: Ore is defined by having a useful mineral concentrated enough to mine profitably.

check.q: Why do some regions have copper and others none?
choices: Copper was placed by ancient people
Copper collects only where specific processes, like hot fluids in cracks, concentrated it
Copper is spread evenly but hidden
check.why: Ore deposits form only where particular geologic processes happened, so they are patchy.

check.q: Why is recycling copper a good idea from a resource point of view?
choices: Recycling makes new copper form underground
Reused copper is just as useful and needs far less energy and digging
check.why: Metal does not wear out, and reusing it avoids the energy and waste of mining new ore.

lessons.title: Fresh Water, Unevenly Shared
lessons.mainIdea: Fresh water is scarce and unevenly spread, so where a place sits in the water cycle decides how much it has.
reading: Northern Illinois sits next to one of the largest bodies of fresh water on the planet. Parts of the American Southwest, at the same latitude, are desert. That is not fairness or luck; it is the water cycle. Rain falls where moist air rises and cools. It does not fall where air sinks and warms, or in the rain shadow behind mountains. People, though, live in both kinds of places.

Water comes from three sources. *Surface water* is lakes and rivers, easy to reach and easy to pollute. Groundwater fills aquifers, cleaner but slow to refill. And a few dry coastal cities remove salt from seawater, which works but takes a great deal of energy. Illinois uses all but the last: Chicago drinks the lake, central Illinois pumps the Mahomet Aquifer, and river towns draw from the Illinois and the Mississippi.

Scarcity comes from use as well as supply. The average American home uses roughly 300 liters of water per person per day, and farms and power plants use far more. In dry regions, aquifers that took thousands of years to fill are being pumped down in decades. Parts of the High Plains aquifer under Kansas and Texas have dropped tens of meters since heavy pumping began. Farmers there are learning to grow crops with less.

Lake Michigan is protected by an agreement among the Great Lakes states and Canadian provinces that limits sending water outside the lakes' basin. Even so, Illinois is allowed only a fixed amount each day, and it must count every liter. Water that seems endless from the shore is carefully rationed on paper.

words.d: water in lakes, rivers and streams on top of the ground
when a place does not have enough usable fresh water for its needs
the whole area of land that drains into a river or lake

look.title: How Much Water Each Great Lake Holds
look.cite: U.S. EPA Great Lakes facts, rounded
look.prompt: Lake Erie is the smallest and shallowest. Why might it be the fastest to show pollution and the fastest to recover?

check.q: Why do deserts exist at the same latitude as rainy places?
choices: The sun is hotter over deserts
Air sinks and warms there, or mountains block the moist air
check.why: Rain needs rising, cooling air; sinking air and rain shadows leave regions dry.

check.q: Which water source is the cleanest but the slowest to refill?
check.why: Groundwater is filtered by rock and soil but recharges slowly, so overpumping lowers it for decades.

check.q: Why does Illinois have to measure how much Lake Michigan water it uses?
choices: An agreement among the Great Lakes states and provinces limits each one's share
The water is owned by Canada
check.why: The Great Lakes are shared, and Illinois is allowed a fixed daily amount under the agreement.

lessons.title: Energy From the Ground and the Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Every energy source has a cost and a benefit, and where it comes from depends on geology and geography.
reading: Flip a switch in Illinois and the electricity comes from a mix: nuclear plants, natural gas, coal, wind turbines and a growing number of solar panels. Illinois gets more of its electricity from nuclear power than any other state, and its flat, windy prairie has made it one of the top wind-power states. Each source exists where it does for a reason.

*Fossil fuels* are ancient sunlight. Coal is the buried remains of swamp forests; oil and natural gas are the remains of tiny sea organisms, cooked and squeezed over millions of years. The Illinois Basin holds one of the largest coal deposits in the country, laid down in the Pennsylvanian swamps. Fossil fuels pack a lot of energy and are easy to store and ship. Burning them also releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants, and they do not regrow.

*Renewable* sources are different. Wind and sunlight arrive every day whether we use them or not, and using them releases no carbon dioxide. But they depend on weather and place. Wind farms need steady wind; solar farms need clear sky. Storing the energy for calm nights takes batteries or other tricks. Hydroelectric dams give steady power but flood valleys. Nuclear plants release no carbon dioxide while running but leave waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years.

There is no free source. Choosing among them means weighing cost, reliability, pollution, land use and safety, and the best mix is different in Illinois than in Arizona or Norway. Science can measure each trade-off. Deciding which ones to accept is something a community has to do.

words.d: coal, oil or natural gas, formed from ancient living things buried for millions of years
a resource, like wind or sunlight, that nature replaces about as fast as it is used
giving up one good thing to get another

look.title: Powering a Town
look.text: A town of 20,000 people on the Illinois prairie needs a new power source. Option A is a natural gas plant that runs day and night. Option B is a wind farm that makes more total energy over a year but nothing on calm days. Option C is both, with batteries.
look.prompt: List one strength and one weakness of each option. Which trade-offs matter most, and who should decide?

check.q: Where did the energy in coal originally come from?
choices: Sunlight captured by ancient swamp plants
check.why: Coal is the buried remains of plants that stored sunlight through photosynthesis.

check.q: What is the main drawback of wind and solar power?
choices: They release a lot of carbon dioxide
They use up a nonrenewable resource
They depend on weather and need storage for calm or dark times
check.why: Wind and sun vary with weather and time of day, so a reliable supply needs storage or backup.

check.q: Why does Illinois have so much wind power?
choices: Its flat, open prairie has steady winds
It has no other energy sources
Wind turbines only work near lakes
check.why: Flat, open land with steady wind is ideal for wind farms.

lessons.title: What Can and Cannot Be Predicted
lessons.mainIdea: Some hazards give warning signs that can be measured; others cannot be timed, only mapped.
reading: Natural *hazards* are not evenly spread either. Illinois does not worry about hurricanes or volcanoes. It does worry about tornadoes, floods, ice storms, heat waves and, in the south, earthquakes. Each hazard has its own physics, and that physics decides how much warning people can get.

Hazards that build up slowly can be forecast. A river flood comes from rain that fell days earlier upstream, so gauges and rain totals give days of notice. A hurricane is tracked for a week by satellite. A volcano usually swells and shakes for weeks before it erupts. Tornadoes give minutes, from radar. Earthquakes give nothing: no signal has ever been found that reliably comes before the rock breaks.

For hazards with no warning, scientists map probability instead. An earthquake hazard map does not say when; it says how likely strong shaking is over, say, the next 50 years. A flood map shows the 100-year floodplain, land with about a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year. That does not mean once a century. It can flood two years in a row.

Illinois keeps a state geological survey and a state water survey partly for this reason. Their job is to measure: how fast the ground shakes at New Madrid, how high the Illinois River rises, how much of the state is floodplain. Good maps come from long records, and long records come from people who kept measuring in the quiet years.

words.d: a natural event that can harm people or property
the flat land next to a river that floods when the river overflows
how likely something is, often written as a percent

look.title: The Hundred-Year Flood
look.text: A family buys a house on the Illinois River. The seller says it is in the 100-year floodplain but adds that it flooded just three years ago, so they are safe for a long time.
look.prompt: Is the seller's reasoning right? What does a 1 percent chance per year actually mean over the next ten years?

check.q: Which hazard can currently be forecast the furthest in advance?
check.why: Hurricanes are tracked by satellite for about a week before landfall.

check.q: What does a 100-year floodplain mean?
choices: It floods exactly once every 100 years
It has not flooded in 100 years
It has about a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year
It is safe for 100 years after a flood
check.why: The label is a yearly probability, about 1 percent, and floods can come in back-to-back years.

check.q: Since earthquakes cannot be predicted, what do scientists produce instead?
choices: Exact dates for the next quake
Maps of how likely strong shaking is over a long period
check.why: Hazard maps give the probability of shaking, which guides building codes and planning.

lessons.title: Building for the Worst Day
lessons.mainIdea: People cannot stop hazards, but they can reduce harm by building, planning and warning based on the evidence.
reading: The same tornado can flatten one town and barely scratch another. The difference is often preparation. Illinois schools drill for tornadoes. Newer buildings in the south of the state have stronger connections between walls and roofs and between the building and its foundation, because of the New Madrid hazard maps. A building code is science turned into rules.

Floods are the costliest hazard in Illinois, and the answers are a mix. Levees hold rivers back, but they push water higher downstream and fail when overtopped. Some towns have done the opposite: after repeated floods, Valmeyer, Illinois, moved its whole town up onto the bluffs in the 1990s. Restoring wetlands lets floodwater spread out and soak in instead of racing downstream. Zoning keeps new houses off the floodplain in the first place.

Warning systems matter as much as walls. Chicago's deadly 1995 heat wave killed hundreds of people, many of them elderly and alone. Since then the city has a heat plan: cooling centers, wellness checks, alerts. The hazard did not change. The response did. Every disaster becomes data for the next plan.

Engineers design with a question: how bad a day should this survive? A stronger building costs more, and no budget can protect against everything. Deciding how much risk to accept is a choice a community makes together, ideally with the hazard maps in front of it.

words.d: the rules for how strong and safe a building must be built
a wall or bank built along a river to keep floodwater out
actions taken ahead of time to reduce the harm from a hazard

look.title: Powell Warns About Water in the West
look.text: In his report on the arid lands of the West, John Wesley Powell argued that most of that region could never be farmed the way the East was, because there was not enough rain, and that settlement should be planned around the limited water that rivers could supply.
look.cite: John Wesley Powell, Report on the Lands of the Arid Region of the United States, 1878, paraphrased
look.prompt: Powell was largely ignored, and cities grew in the desert anyway. What kinds of evidence did he have, and why might people have refused to act on it?

check.q: Why do buildings in southern Illinois follow stricter earthquake rules than those in the north?
choices: The New Madrid hazard maps show a higher chance of strong shaking there
The soil is softer in the north
The rules are the same everywhere
check.why: Building codes are set from hazard maps, and the New Madrid zone raises the risk in the south.

check.q: What is one drawback of levees?
choices: They push floodwater higher downstream and can fail if overtopped
check.why: Levees keep water off one place by sending it elsewhere, and they can be overtopped in a big flood.

check.q: After the 1995 Chicago heat wave, what changed?
choices: The city built a giant air conditioner
The city created plans for cooling centers, checks and alerts
check.why: The hazard stayed the same; the response system was built so fewer people would die next time.

sections.title: How People Change Land, Water and Air

lessons.title: Footprints on the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Farming, cities and mining have remade most of Illinois's land, and the changes ripple into water and wildlife.
reading: Illinois calls itself the Prairie State, but almost none of the prairie is left. Before 1800, tall grass prairie covered more than half the state. Today less than one tenth of one percent of that original prairie survives, in scattered patches like cemetery corners and railroad edges. The rest is corn, soybeans, roads and towns. Few places on Earth have been changed so completely.

The change was not all loss. Prairie soil is among the richest in the world, and Illinois farms feed millions. But bare soil washes away in rain. Fertilizer that crops do not use runs into ditches, then rivers, then the Gulf of Mexico, where it feeds algae that use up the oxygen and create a dead zone each summer. Illinois and the Mississippi basin states are among the largest sources of that runoff.

Cities change land differently. Pavement and roofs shed rain instead of soaking it up, so storms send water rushing into streams all at once. Chicago built one of the world's largest tunnel and reservoir systems to hold that runoff so it would not flood basements and overflow into the lake. That is a *human impact* that is also an engineering answer to an earlier human impact.

The good news is that impacts can be measured and reduced. Farmers plant cover crops to hold soil in winter. Prairie strips along field edges catch runoff. Cities require green roofs and rain gardens. None of it restores 1800, but all of it shows up in cleaner water downstream.

words.d: a change to the environment caused by people
rainwater that flows over the ground into streams instead of soaking in
an area of water with so little oxygen that most sea life cannot live there

look.title: Two Fields in a Storm
look.text: Two neighboring fields get the same hard April rain. One was plowed bare last fall. The other was planted with a winter cover crop of rye that is now ankle high. You look at the ditch below each field after the storm.
look.prompt: Predict what each ditch looks like. Where did the soil and fertilizer go in each case?

check.q: About how much of Illinois's original prairie remains?
choices: Less than one tenth of one percent
check.why: Farming and cities replaced nearly all the prairie; only tiny scattered patches survive.

check.q: How does fertilizer used in Illinois affect the Gulf of Mexico?
choices: It has no effect that far away
Runoff carries it down the Mississippi, feeding algae that use up oxygen
check.why: Nutrient runoff travels downriver and fuels algae blooms that create a low-oxygen dead zone.

check.q: Why do cities flood faster than farmland during the same storm?
choices: Pavement and roofs shed water instead of soaking it up
check.why: Hard surfaces send rain straight to streams and sewers instead of into the ground.

lessons.title: Clearing the Air and Water
lessons.mainIdea: Air and water pollution were measured, traced to their sources and cut by laws and engineering, which shows that impacts can be reversed.
reading: In the 1960s the Cuyahoga River in Ohio was so coated with oil and debris that it caught fire. Lake Erie was declared dying. Chicago's air was thick with coal smoke. None of that is normal today. The change did not come from luck. It came from measurement, then rules, then engineering.

Scientists learned to trace pollution to its source. Sulfur from coal smoke was linked to *acid rain* that killed fish in lakes hundreds of kilometers downwind. Phosphates in detergents were linked to algae choking Lake Erie. Lead from gasoline was found in children's blood. Once the source was clear, laws in the 1970s required cleaner fuels, scrubbers on smokestacks and treatment of sewage before it entered rivers.

The results are measurable. Lead in American children's blood fell by more than 90 percent after leaded gasoline was phased out. Sulfur dioxide from power plants dropped sharply after limits were set. Lake Erie's fish came back, though algae blooms still return in warm years from farm runoff. Pollution did not vanish, but the worst of it was reversed within a generation.

The lesson is not that the problems are solved. It is that the method works. Measure, find the source, act, and measure again. Air quality monitors across Chicago still report ozone and fine particles every hour, so anyone can check whether today's air is safe to run in.

words.d: harmful substances added to air, water or land by people
rain made acidic by sulfur and nitrogen gases from burning fuel
measuring something regularly over time to watch for change

look.title: Carson on Poisons in the Water
look.text: Rachel Carson warned that chemicals sprayed on farms and forests did not stay where they were put. They washed into streams and groundwater, moved through the food chain and turned up in places, and in living things, far from where anyone had used them.
look.cite: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, 1962, paraphrased
look.prompt: Carson's argument depended on the water cycle. How does something sprayed on a field end up in a lake or a bird?

check.q: What was the first step in cleaning up acid rain?
choices: Measuring the pollution and tracing it to sulfur from smokestacks
check.why: Scientists first showed that sulfur from burning coal was making rain acidic far downwind.

check.q: What happened to lead levels in American children after leaded gasoline was phased out?
choices: They fell by more than 90 percent
check.why: Removing the source cut blood lead levels dramatically within a generation.

check.q: Why do Lake Erie algae blooms still return in warm years?
choices: Farm runoff still carries nutrients into the lake
Detergents are still full of phosphate
check.why: Point sources like detergents were controlled, but spread-out runoff from farms is harder to stop.

lessons.title: More People, More Demand
lessons.mainIdea: Human impact grows with both how many people there are and how much each person uses.
reading: In 1800 about one billion people lived on Earth. In 2022 the world passed eight billion. Each person needs water, food, energy and space, so more people means more demand. But numbers are only half of it. A person in a wealthy country uses many times the energy and materials of a person in a poor one. Impact is people multiplied by *consumption* per person.

That is why some of the biggest changes to Earth have come from a small share of its people. A car, a large house, air travel and a diet heavy in meat each carry a large footprint in land, water and carbon. The same eight billion people could press on the planet much harder or much more lightly depending on how they live and what technology they use.

Technology cuts both ways. Fertilizer and better seeds let farms feed billions on the same land, sparing forests. But the same fertilizer feeds the Gulf dead zone. LED bulbs use a fraction of the electricity of old bulbs, so lighting the world costs less energy than it did. Efficiency is the quiet reason many rich countries now use less energy per person than they did decades ago.

Population growth itself is slowing. In most countries, families have grown smaller as children survive, girls go to school and cities grow. Scientists expect the world's population to level off later this century. The open question is not only how many people, but how each of us will live.

words.d: the amount of resources a person or group uses
the total land, water and energy it takes to support a person's way of life
getting the same result while using less energy or material

look.title: World Population Through Time
look.cite: United Nations estimates, rounded
look.prompt: How long did it take to add the first billion after 1800? The most recent billion? What does the pattern show?

check.q: Which two things together determine how much people press on Earth's resources?
choices: Number of people and consumption per person
Number of people and the size of Earth
Consumption per person and the weather
The number of countries and their age
check.why: Impact is population multiplied by how much each person uses.

check.q: Why can a smaller number of people sometimes have a bigger environmental impact?
choices: They use far more energy and materials per person
check.why: High consumption per person, like cars and air travel, multiplies the impact of each individual.

check.q: How does an LED bulb reduce human impact?
choices: It gives the same light using much less electricity

lessons.title: The Greenhouse Effect
lessons.mainIdea: Certain gases in the air trap heat leaving Earth, which keeps the planet warm enough to live on and warms it more as they increase.
reading: Sunlight passes through the air, warms the ground, and the ground gives that heat back as invisible infrared radiation. Most gases in the air let infrared pass. A few do not. Water vapor, *carbon dioxide* and methane absorb it and send part of it back down. That trapping is the *greenhouse effect*, and without it Earth's average temperature would be about 33 degrees Celsius colder, well below freezing.

The effect was measured in a lab long before anyone worried about it. In the 1850s and 1860s, an Irish physicist named John Tyndall shone heat through tubes of different gases and found that carbon dioxide and water vapor blocked it strongly while oxygen and nitrogen barely did. In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling the carbon dioxide in the air would warm the planet by several degrees. He thought it would take thousands of years.

It did not. Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that was locked underground for millions of years. In 1958 Charles Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide on a mountain in Hawaii, far from any city. The number was about 315 parts per million. It has risen every single year since and passed 420 parts per million in the 2020s. Bubbles of ancient air trapped in ice cores show it is higher now than at any time in at least 800,000 years.

The physics is not in doubt. More carbon dioxide traps more heat; that is the same measurement Tyndall made. The open scientific questions are about how fast, how much, and how the oceans, clouds and ice will respond. Those are the questions climate scientists spend their careers measuring.

lessons.title: The Evidence for a Warming World
lessons.mainIdea: Many independent measurements, from thermometers to ice to sea level, all point the same way: Earth is warming, and the added carbon dioxide is the main cause.
reading: No single thermometer proves a planet is warming. Thousands do. Weather stations, ships, buoys and satellites all record temperature, and separate teams in different countries have combined them. They agree: Earth's average surface temperature is now roughly 1.1 to 1.2 degrees Celsius warmer than in the late 1800s, and most of that rise has come since 1975. The last ten years include the warmest years ever recorded.

Other lines of evidence point the same way, and they do not depend on thermometers. Glaciers on every continent are shrinking. Arctic sea ice in late summer covers far less area than it did in 1980. Sea level has risen more than 20 centimeters since 1900 as warm water expands and ice melts. Spring comes earlier: plants bloom and birds migrate days sooner than a century ago. Lake Michigan freezes less often than it used to.

Could something else be the cause? Scientists have checked. The sun's output has been measured by satellite since the 1970s and has not increased. Volcanoes cool the planet briefly, not warm it. Natural cycles like El Niño move heat around but do not add it. The only change that fits the size, timing and pattern of the warming is the extra heat-trapping gas, and the pattern includes a fingerprint: the upper atmosphere is cooling while the surface warms, which is what added greenhouse gases predict.

Being honest about uncertainty matters here. Scientists do not know exactly how much warming a given amount of carbon dioxide will finally cause, or how quickly ice sheets will respond. They express that as a range. But the direction, and the cause, are as solid as anything in Earth science. Illinois's own climate records show the shift: warmer winters, heavier downpours and a growing season that has grown longer.

lessons.title: Designing a Lighter Footprint
lessons.mainIdea: Reducing human impact means measuring it, designing solutions that cut it and monitoring to see whether they work.
reading: Engineers treat impact as a design problem. Start with a measurement: how much carbon, water or waste does this thing cause? Then redesign to cut it, test, and measure again. Chicago's City Hall has a garden on its roof that cools the building and soaks up rain. Illinois wind farms now produce electricity that once came from coal. Neither happened by wishing; each was designed, priced and checked.

Solutions come in a few kinds. Some replace a source: solar and wind instead of coal, electric buses instead of diesel. Some use less: insulation, LED lights, efficient engines. Some capture what is released: catchment basins for runoff, filters on smokestacks, forests and wetlands that pull carbon dioxide out of the air. Some adapt: raising roads, planting heat-tolerant trees, moving Valmeyer up the bluff. Most real plans use all four.

Every solution has trade-offs too. Wind turbines need land and can kill birds. Batteries need mined lithium and cobalt. Nuclear plants avoid carbon but produce long-lived waste. Choosing well means comparing the whole footprint of each option, not just one piece of it. That comparison is science; the choice is a decision for citizens.

The last step is the one that makes it science: *monitoring*. Satellites map ice, forests and sea level every day. Argo floats drift through the oceans measuring heat. Mauna Loa still reports carbon dioxide every month. Chicago's air monitors and Lake Michigan's water tests keep running. Without those numbers, no one would know whether any of the solutions worked. With them, we do.
